title: Composite infrared and radio image of 30 Doradus
caption: The Tarantula Nebula (30 Doradus), imaged by ALMA, the Very Large Telescope and VISTA
credit: ESO, ALMA (ESO/NAOJ/NRAO)/Wong et al., ESO/M.-R. Cioni/VISTA Magellanic Cloud survey. Acknowledgment: Cambridge Astronomical Survey Unit

recognition.text: Official ESO press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: Bright red-yellow streaks lie across a background of bright stars and light pink clouds of hot gas in this composite of 30 Doradus, the star-forming region also called the Tarantula Nebula.

The background is itself a blend of infrared images from the HAWK-I instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope and from VISTA, the Visible and Infrared Survey Telescope for Astronomy. The infrared view shows the stars and the hot gas around them.

The streaks come from radio observations with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, ALMA. They trace cold, dense gas, the kind of material that could collapse and form new stars. Such gas is the raw material from which stars are made. The nebula's web-like tangle of gas clouds is also what earned it its spidery nickname.

understand.summary: This combines near-infrared images from HAWK-I on the VLT and VISTA with ALMA millimeter observations of carbon monoxide. The ALMA data appear as the red-yellow streaks, and the infrared data form the background of stars and pinkish gas.
